catalog_locator: Sec. 3.6 'Stress', pp. 162-163, incl. fn. 102 p. 162 and examples (32)-(33); fn. 67 p. 109; sec. 3.7 Summary p. 164 with fn. 103; compound example (11) pp. 110-111
catalog_quote: Stress or prominence occurs on the final syllable of the stem. It does not shift when a suffix or clitic is added to the stem. ... Stress is predominantly indicated through increased intensity occasionally accompanied by a slightly lengthened vowel. In monomorphemic words, stress occurs on the final syllable as can be seen in (32). ... In multimorphemic words, the stressed syllable is always the final syllable of the stem, even when an affix or clitic is added. Note the examples in (33) below. In (33a) a prefix is added to the stem and the stress remains on the final syllable of the word. In (33b-f), clitics are added to the end of the stem and the stress remains on the final syllable of the stem, it does not shift to the final syllable of the word. ... The actual placement of the stem in the surface grammatical word and the number of affixes is irrelevant. Stress placement is only dependent on the stem. All syllable types can occur in stressed and unstressed syllables. There is no indication of vowel reduction or tone loss on unstressed syllables. ... Although stress is active in the licensing of tone in many Oto-Manguean languages, there is no indication of this effect in Soyaltepec Mazatec. Because stress is very regular and does not enter into the tone system, it will not be marked in the remainder of the dissertation.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the last syllable of the stem: word-final in monomorphemic words and in prefixed words, but enclitics/suffixes (negative -hi, possessive -na, -ʔɛ, -ɲa, modal -ra) are extrametrical and stress stays on the stem-final syllable; in compounds stress is on the final syllable of the whole compound stem. Stress is weight-insensitive, cued by intensity (and slight lengthening), independent of the tone system; nasal vowels are (with listed exceptions) restricted to the stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Fn. 102 (p. 162): 'Secondary stress can also be found in some words, but further investigation is beyond the scope of this paper.' No placement rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: None to stress placement itself; author notes (fn. 102) that because stress is 'constant and immovable' it might better be called a prominent syllable. Exceptions discussed concern nasal vowels occurring outside the stressed syllable (certain enclitics, first members of compounds). Fn. 103: one tone sandhi process (sec. 5.2.2) may involve floating-tone attraction to the stressed syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem within the grammatical word (prefix + stem + enclitics); statements based on elicited words, frames, sentences and texts from six speakers of San Miguel Soyaltepec municipality (Temascal area), Oaxaca, recorded 2005-2009. Language is tonal (4 levels + contours); stress described as 'not a very active process' and unmarked in the rest of the work.
new_statements.identity_note: Beal's data are from six speakers in the San Miguel Soyaltepec municipality (Temascal / Miguel Alemán dam resettlement area), Oaxaca — Soyaltepec Mazatec proper, ISO vmp, glottocode soya1237; no sub-dialect distinction drawn.

new_statements.relation_note: Same source and same statement as the existing_statement (Beal 2013 is the published SIL e-Book edition of this 2011 UT Arlington dissertation; the front matter of the on-disk PDF reads 'The University of Texas at Arlington, 2011'). The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so this work fills it: stem-final stress. Locator refinement: sec. 3.6 begins on printed p. 161 (p. 180), not p. 162; fn. 67 is on printed p. 108, not 109. The 2011 UTA copy itself could not be downloaded (handle 10106/9539 redirects to the migrated mavmatrix.uta.edu root; the mavmatrix search could not be reached by automated download), so the reading rests on the 2013 edition.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress/prominence falls on the final syllable of the stem (root plus derivational material), regardless of prefixes, suffixes or enclitics; in monomorphemic words this is simply the last syllable, but enclitics added after the stem do not attract stress, so the stressed syllable is not always word-final. Stress is cued by intensity and slight vowel lengthening, is constant and immovable, and its only phonological effect is licensing nasal vowels; tone is essentially independent of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Fn. 102 (p. 161): 'Secondary stress can also be found in some words, but further investigation is beyond the scope of this paper.' No placement given.
new_statements.exceptions: None to placement. Nasality restriction to the stressed syllable has three exceptions (nasal enclitics, some enclitics, first members of compounds keep nasality after losing primary stress, ex. 33f). Fn. 103 (p. 163) and sec. 5.2.2 hypothesise that a floating tone docks preferentially to the stressed (stem-final) syllable rather than to an unstressed suffix; 'More research is needed to confirm the association.' No vowel reduction or tone loss on unstressed syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Beal describes Soyaltepec Mazatec (ISO vmp) as spoken in San Miguel Soyaltepec, Oaxaca; no sub-dialect distinction is made in the stress section. The listed work (2011 UT Arlington dissertation) and the on-disk file (2013 SIL e-Book 53) are the same text in two editions.

tone_statements.citation: Biber, Douglas. 1981. The lexical representation of contour tones. International Journal of American Linguistics 47(4): 271-282.
tone_statements.quote: Thus the level-sequence analysis is overwhelmingly the superior analysis for this dialect of Mazatec. ... Four separate types of processes were referred to in order to demonstrate that the gliding tones of Soyaltepec Mazatec are a phonemic sequence of level tones, rather than phonemic contour tones. These processes are: (1) spreading (absorption), (2) shifting, (3) raising or lowering one of the endpoints of a gliding tone, and (4) combining a level floating tone with another tone (level or gliding) to form a gliding tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 277, end of sec. 1 and opening of sec. 2; inventory in Table 1, p. 274; floating tones p. 277
tone_statements.summary: Argues from Pike's 1956 data that Soyaltepec Mazatec has four level tones (1 highest to 4) and that its many gliding tones are sequences of two level tones on one syllable; posits floating tones.
